stemBlocks.value: H, J, K, L and M lie on a circle with centre O. MK is a diameter and MK is parallel to HJ; MJ = JL and angle JMK = 38°. Explain, giving a reason, why (a) angle HJM = 38° and (b) angle MJK = 90°.
Think first: Each answer needs one named theorem, not a calculation — say which lines or which theorem create the angle.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p246-q12 from workbook page 246.

solutionSteps.instruction: Identify the transversal joining the two parallel lines.

contentBlocks.value: MK is parallel to HJ and the chord MJ crosses both of them
Result: MJ is a transversal of two parallel lines

solutionSteps.instruction: Name the relationship between angle JMK and angle HJM.

contentBlocks.value: They lie on opposite sides of the transversal MJ and between the parallels MK and HJ, so they are alternate angles

solutionSteps.instruction: Look at the angle that the diameter MK subtends at J.

contentBlocks.value: J lies on the circumference and MK is a diameter, so MJK is an angle in a semicircle

strategyBlocks.value: Treat MJ as a transversal cutting the parallel lines MK and HJ for part (a), and use the diameter MK subtending an angle at J for part (b).

finalAnswerBlocks.value: (a) ∠HJM = 38° because MK is parallel to HJ and MJ is a transversal, so ∠HJM and ∠JMK are alternate angles (often called Z-angles), which are equal.  (b) ∠MJK = 90° because MK is a diameter and J lies on the circumference, so ∠MJK is the angle in a semicircle, which is a right angle.

whyThisWorks.value: Parallel lines transfer an angle from one place in a figure to another without changing its size, which is why the 38° at M reappears at J. The semicircle result is really the angle-at-the-centre theorem in a special case: the diameter makes a straight angle of 180° at the centre, so the angle it makes at the circumference is half of that, 90°.
